headline: A wildfire destroys 640 buildings in one afternoon

sources.title: Old Trails fire in northwest Spokane destroys 640 structures
The Wildfire Disaster Unfolding In Spokane, Washington
Fires on more than 250,000 acres of Washington state prompt evacuations
600+ structures lost, thousands of people are evacuated | Spokane County Wildfires: 10 a.m. Update (video, KREM 2 News)

chunks.text: A [[wildfire]] {{broke out}} on Saturday, August 1, on open ground west of Spokane, in the eastern half of Washington state. Within hours it had {{torn through}} whole streets on the edge of the city. By Sunday the fire chief for the district said 640 [[structures]] had {{burned down}}, most of them houses, and many of them inside the Spokane city [[limits]]. No deaths have been reported.

verbs.wrong: To spread from tree to tree
verbs.why: A fight can break out in a crowded bar, and a fever can break out overnight. The wildfire broke out on open ground west of Spokane before the wind carried it into the city.

verbs.correct: To move through a place fast and destroy it
verbs.wrong: To burn slowly along the forest floor
verbs.why: A tornado can tear through a small town, and a virus can tear through a crowded school. Driven by strong wind, the fire tore through whole streets on the edge of Spokane.

verbs.correct: To be destroyed completely by fire
verbs.wrong: To be damaged by heat but still stand
verbs.why: An old barn can burn down in minutes, and a candle slowly burns down to nothing. About 640 structures burned down in one afternoon near Spokane, most of them family homes.

chunks.text: The wind was the biggest factor in what happened that day. [[Gusts]] {{picked up}} to between 35 and 45 miles an hour and held there for hours, pushing the flames northeast into a state park. From there the fire [[jumped]] a river, climbed the [[bluffs]] on the [[far side]] and reached the first houses. [[Crews]] could not {{hold back}} a [[front]] moving that fast, and they could not {{put out}} what was already burning, so they worked instead on getting people away from it.

verbs.why: Wind picks up before a big storm, and traffic picks up after a busy game ends. Gusts picked up to 45 miles an hour and pushed the flames northeast into a state park.

verbs.wrong: To make a fire spread even faster
verbs.why: A dam holds back a flooding river, and security holds back an excited crowd. Firefighters could not hold back a wind driven fire moving that fast.

verbs.correct: To stop a fire from burning
verbs.wrong: To carry water to the fire line
verbs.why: Firefighters put out house fires, and campers put out a fire before leaving a campsite. Crews could not put out flames that were already spreading through entire neighborhoods.

chunks.text: Thousands of people were {{moved out}} of their homes across Spokane County, some with a few minutes' [[notice]]. The city {{set up}} its main [[shelter]] in the [[convention center]] downtown. The mayor declared a city [[emergency]]. The governor declared one for the whole state, {{called in}} the [[National Guard]] and {{brought in}} a [[burn ban]] that [[covers]] every county. The cause of the fire is still under [[investigation]].

verbs.correct: To make people leave a place
verbs.wrong: To start living in a new home
verbs.why: Officials move out residents before a flood, and workers move out families during a gas leak. Thousands of people were moved out of their homes across Spokane County with only a few minutes notice.

verbs.wrong: To pay the cost of something
verbs.why: Campers set up a tent before dark, and cities set up shelters after a disaster. Spokane set up its main shelter inside the downtown convention center.
Coaches call in a substitute player during a tough game, and mayors call in extra police for a large event. The governor called in the National Guard once wildfires spread across the state.

verbs.wrong: To explain a rule to the public
verbs.why: Schools bring in guest speakers, and cities sometimes bring in new rules during an emergency. The governor brought in a burn ban that covers every county in the state.

chunks.text: Spokane [[is not alone]]. Fires across Washington now {{add up}} to more than 250,000 [[acres]], and smoke has {{built up}} over seven counties [[badly enough for]] [[air quality]] warnings. Eastern Washington has spent the summer in record [[drought]], and [[forecasters]] expect dry air and more wind [[rather than]] rain. A separate fire north of the city started from a single [[ember]] and took three more houses. What made Saturday different was not that a fire started, but that the wind carried it into a place where people live.

verbs.correct: To reach a total when combined
verbs.why: Small daily expenses add up over a year, and little mistakes can add up fast. Fires across Washington now add up to more than 250,000 burned acres.
Dust builds up on a shelf, and pressure builds up before a big exam. Smoke built up over seven counties until air quality warnings were needed.

mainIdea.s: Strong winds pushed a wildfire into homes near Spokane, and 640 structures burned down in one afternoon. Crews could not hold back the flames, so they focused on moving people out instead.
mainIdea.why: Strong winds pushed the fire fast into homes, and crews could not hold it back. About 640 structures burned down in one afternoon near Spokane.

mainIdea.s: A wildfire near Spokane destroyed 640 buildings in one afternoon as strong winds pushed flames into homes. Investigators say the cause was a campfire that campers left burning nearby that week.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the cause of the fire has not been found. The article says the cause of the fire is still under investigation.

mainIdea.s: State officials in Washington are reviewing a new plan to raise wildfire funding for the coming year. Lawmakers hope the extra money pays for more aircraft and more firefighting crews.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a state funding plan for next year's fire season, not the fire that hit Spokane in one afternoon.
